lesson.text: Quick memory: in history this year, how did the Persian kings treat the many peoples of their empire? (Most kept their own languages, customs and beliefs.) Today: the many cultures that live side by side, and what we all share.

A culture is the way of life a group shares: its languages, food, clothes, music, stories, festivals and beliefs. Everyone has a culture, and many people belong to more than one: a family's, a country's, a school's.

About 7,000 languages are spoken in the world today. People greet in many ways: a handshake, or a bow in Japan. In India, 'namaste' with hands pressed together; in parts of Europe, a kiss on the cheek.

People hold many beliefs. Among the biggest religions are Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism and Sikhism, and many people follow no religion. Respect means we never mock anyone's beliefs, even when we do not share them.

Many festivals are about light, food and family: Diwali, Hanukkah and Christmas bring lights in dark months; Eid al-Fitr ends a month of fasting with a feast; Lunar New Year and Nowruz welcome a new year.

Under the differences, we share a lot: we all need food, safety, friends and family; we laugh, play, tell stories and make music. Finding what we share helps us get along; learning our differences makes life richer.
A stereotype is an idea that everyone in a group is the same. Stereotypes are unfair, because every person is different. Ask, listen and get to know people for who they are.
Try it in the world: plan a festival square in your world where friends can share a food, a game or a greeting from their family's culture. Next: courage and doing the right thing.

exercises.hint: Languages, food, music, festivals and beliefs.
choices: the way of life a group shares
exercises.explain: A culture is the way of life a group shares.

exercises.hint: Does your family have its own food, stories or celebrations?
exercises.explain: True: everyone shares a way of life with others.

exercises.prompt: About how many languages are spoken in the world today?
exercises.hint: It is a lot, but far fewer than the number of people.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a Jewish festival of lights?
exercises.hint: Diwali is also a festival of lights, but a Hindu, Sikh and Jain one.
exercises.explain: Hanukkah, a Jewish festival of lights.

exercises.prompt: Respecting a belief means you must share it.
exercises.hint: Can you respect a friend's belief that is not yours?
exercises.explain: False: respect means never mocking it, even when you do not share it.

exercises.prompt: Match each festival to what it marks.
matches: a new year set by the Moon
the end of a month of fasting
exercises.hint: Two of them welcome a new year.
exercises.explain: Eid al-Fitr ends the fast; Diwali is a festival of lights; Nowruz and Lunar New Year welcome a new year.

exercises.hint: Is every person in a group the same?
choices: an idea that everyone in a group is the same
exercises.explain: A stereotype says everyone in a group is the same, which is unfair.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: differs between cultures, or shared by all people?
exercises.hint: Would it be the same everywhere in the world?
exercises.explain: Differs: language, greetings, festival foods. Shared: needing food and safety, caring about family and friends.

exercises.prompt: A new classmate eats with chopsticks. What is respectful?
exercises.hint: How would you like people to react to your ways?
choices: be curious: ask them to show you how
tell them to use a fork
exercises.explain: Be curious and kind: asking to learn shows respect.

exercises.prompt: Many people belong to more than one culture.
exercises.hint: Think of a family's, a country's and a school's culture.
exercises.explain: True: a person can share several cultures at once.

exercises.hint: Are all the people you know from one place the same?
exercises.explain: Every person is different, so judging someone by a group is unfair.

exercises.prompt: Two friends celebrate different festivals. What could they do?
exercises.hint: Learning about differences makes life richer.
choices: invite each other and learn about both
exercises.explain: They can invite each other and learn about both festivals.

exercises.prompt: Which is a respectful way to talk about beliefs you do not share?
exercises.explain: Listen, ask questions kindly and never mock.

exercises.prompt: Put these steps of welcoming a newcomer in order.
items: ask their name and how to say it
exercises.explain: Say hello, learn their name, show them around, then invite them to play.

exercises.prompt: Learning about other cultures can make life richer.
exercises.hint: Think of new foods, games and stories.
exercises.explain: True: new foods, stories, music and friends make life richer.

exercises.prompt: Match each greeting to a place where it is common.
exercises.hint: Card 2 names a greeting for each place.
exercises.explain: A bow is common in Japan, namaste with hands pressed together in India, and a kiss on the cheek in parts of Europe.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sentences: a fair way to think about people, or a stereotype?
items: Everyone from that town is rude.
I'll get to know Sam first.
People in any group are different.
exercises.hint: A stereotype says everyone in a group is the same.
exercises.explain: Stereotypes: everyone from a town is rude, all boys hate dancing, girls can't play football. Fair: getting to know Sam, and remembering that every person in a group is different.

exercises.prompt: Match each festival to how it is celebrated.
matches: a feast after a month's fast
exercises.hint: Think of lights, fasting and new years.
exercises.explain: Diwali: lamps and lights in autumn. Eid al-Fitr: a feast after a month of fasting. Hanukkah: candles lit over eight nights. Lunar New Year: welcoming a new year.
